sentences.text:
Vide this judgment, I propose to dispose off the instant appeal filed u/s 70 of The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 ("FSS Act" in short) against the impugned order dated 28.10.2019 passed by the Adjudicating Officer/Additional District Magistrate (New Delhi)("ADM" in short), whereby a consolidated penalty of Rs.20,000/ was imposed on appellants no.1 to 3, penalty of Rs.50,000/
was imposed on appellant no.4 and penalty of Rs.1,00,000/ was imposed on appellants no.5 & 6 for selling/storing/manufacturing the misbranded product.
2.

The facts in brief are that Sh.Bal Mukund, Food Safety Officer("FSO" in short) purchased the item "Tomato Ketchup" from FBOcumManager Sh.Raj Mal Thakur S/o Late Sh.Het Ram, M/s Fujiya Restaurant, 12/48, Malcha Marge Market, New Delhi110021 on 04.01.2018 as per due procedure for analysis under the provisions of FSS Act & Regulation 2011.

The Food Analyst vide his report no.FSS/21/2018 dated 18.01.2018 opined that the sample is misbranded because there is violation of Regulation No.2.2.2.5(i) of The Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling)
Regulations, 2011 ["FSS (P&L) Regulations" in short].

sentences.text: The Food Analyst also reported about label class title with specific name or recognised international number system for preservatives was not declared on the label.

The appellant no.1 is FBO cum Assistant Manager of M/s Fujiya Restaurant(appellant no.3 FBO firm), appellant no.2 is partner of appellant no.3, appellant no.4 is proprietor to supplier firm to appellant no.3, appellant no.5 is nominee of appellant no.6(manufacturing company/supplier to appellant no.4).

The FSO filed a complaint before the Ld.ADM, New Delhi under 3.1.1(3) of The Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011("FSS Rules" in short) against the appellants for adjudication of the offence u/S 23(1), 26(1), 26(2)(ii), 27(1) and 27(2)(c) r/w Section 3(1) (zf) (C ) (i) of FSS Act alongwith violation of Regulation No.2.2.2.5(i) of FSS (P&L) Regulations which is punishable u/S 52 of FSS Act.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011("FSS Rules
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: In Accordance with the rules, the FBO was served the notice under Rule 3.1.1.(3) of FSS Rules alongwith copy of the report of Food Analyst, affording him an opportunity of being heard.
Ld . ADM
vide impugned order dated 28.10.2019 found the appellants guilty and imposed the penalty as mentioned above.

3. Aggrieved by the impugned order, the appellants have filed the present appeal challenging the impugned order on the grounds that the Ld.ADM did not appreciate the law that the offence of misbranding under Regulation No.2.2.2.5(i) of FSS (P&L) Regulations is made out only when food additive is added to food article and its INS number is not declared on the label.
In this case, in the Tomato Ketchup class II preservative was neither added by manufacturer nor it was found in the sample by the Food Analyst.
Therefore, it is not the case that food additive was added in the sample and INS number was not mentioned on the label.

Merely because superfluous wrongful declaration of food additive, which is class II preservative which was not even added to Tomato Ketchup and was not found in sample by Food Analyst, there was no point of giving any INS number.

It has been submitted that in this case, Acetic acid(INS260) which not only acts as acidifying agent but also as class I preservative was used to preserve the Tomato Ketchup by the manufacturer instead of class II preservative, therefore, writing of INS number of class II preservative was not required to be printed as per law and hence, not written/printed.
It has been submitted that the directions of FSSAI for minor labeling offences was not considered which u/S 16(5) of FSS Act are binding upon the Commissioners of Food Safety and other stakeholders.
It has been submitted that the appellants no.1 to 4 were entitled to defense of due diligence u/S 80 of FSS Act but the same has not been granted.

It has been further submitted that the Delhi Food Laboratory in which this sample Shri Rajmal Thakur S/O Late Shri Het Ram vs Food Safety Officer on 19 August, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/45818632/
2 commodity was analysed and issued analytical report in this case, was not legally competent lab to analyze the samples of food under FSS Act as per Section 43 of FSS Act as the same is neither NABL Accredited nor notified in Official Gazettee as per provisions of Section 3 (1)(p) FSS Act.

sentences.text: Ld. ADM has also not adjudicated the validity of lab as per law and application for summoning of Food Analyst for cross examination was also ignored which is prejudicial to appellants.

Moreover, report of Food Analyst is also not admissible as per provisions of FSS Act unless proved by the Food Analyst as the same is not conclusive as per Evidence Act unlike PFA Act 1954 which now stands repealed.
Therefore, it should not have been read in evidence against the appellants for imposing any penalty.

4. Ld.Counsel for the appellants has submitted that since the Class II preservative which is a Food additive not found present in the sample by the Food Analyst, therefore, non writing of class title with international numbering system, looses its significance and therefore, there is no case of misbranding.

It was also stated that when FSO took the sample, it was in sealed state and not tempered one in any manner and was in the state as were manufactured and supplied by appellants no.5 &6 to appellants no.1 to 4 with valid invoices and therefore, there is complete compliance of defense of due diligence as per Section 80(B) (2)
(a) (i) and (ii) d (i) and (e) and therefore, appellants no.1 to 4 are entitled to be given benefit in this regard.

The appellants also took the plea that the Food Lab at Delhi where the sample was analysed was neither NABL accredited nor the same was notified as per Section 43 FSS Act.
5.
Per contra, Ld.Chief PP has submitted that due opportunity was given to the appellants to file an appeal against the report of Food Analyst.

However, this opportunity was not availed and therefore,
the report of Food Analyst was duly accepted.
It has been submitted that the Ld.ADM has duly appreciated the facts and rightly punished the appellants.

6. Thus, the case of the appellants can be summed up by saying that since there was no class II preservative, therefore, nonmentioning of INS number on the label would not bring the case within the ambit of misbranding.
The second contention is that the defence of due diligence as provided u/S 80 FSS Act should have been given to the appellants no.1 to 4.

The case of the department/respondent can be summed up by saying that the provision of FSS Act are required to be adhered strictly and any deviation from the requirements of this Act, has to be adjudicated in accordance with law.
It has further been submitted that the purpose of Act is primarily to defend the rights of the consumer and therefore, it needs strict interpretation.
7. I have heard the submission and perused the record carefully.

8. In State of Kerala Vs. Parameswaram Pillai Vasudevan Nair, 1975 Cri LJ 97, it was interalia held as under:
"14.The

sentences.text: 3 The consumer's legitimate ignorance and his almost total dependence on the fairness and competence of those who supply his daily needs have made him a ready target for exploitation.
The Act is intended to protect him against outright frauds.
15. The Act does not make a distinction between cases coming under it on the basis of the degree of adulteration.
It does not provide for aggravation of offence based on the extent of contamination.
The offence and punishment are the same whether the adulteration is great or small.

Food pollution, even if it be only to the slightest extent,
if continued in practice, would adversely affect the health of every man, woman and child in the country.

Hence even marginal or border line variations of the prescribed standards under the Act are matters of serious concern for all and as public interests are involved in them, the maxim, de minimis non curat lex law does not concern itself about trifles, does not apply to them.
16. The standard fixed under the Act is one that is certain.
If it is varied to any extent the certainty of a general standard would be replaced by the vagaries of a fluctuating standard.
The disadvantages of the resulting unpredictability, uncertainty and impossibility of arriving at fair and consistent decisions, are great.
17. The Act does not provide for exemption of marginal or border line variations of the standard from the operation of the Act.
In such circumstances to condone such variations on the ground that they are negligible is virtually to alter the standard itself fixed under the Act.
18. The standards of qualities of the articles have been fixed by the Government under the provisions of the Act after due deliberation and after consulting a committee of competent men.
It is for them to give due allowance for probable errors before fixing a standard.
They may have done it also.
There is no reason to assume otherwise.

Therefore the conclusion is that for an article of food when a standard has been fixed under the Act it has to be observed in every detail."
9. Hon'ble Supreme Court after taking into account all the judgments on this issue in Raj Kumar Vs.
State of Uttar Pradesh (2019) 9 SCC 427, interalia held as under: "7.We are of the considered view that once standards are laid down by the legislature then those standards have to be followed.

sentences.text: In items like milk which is a primary food, under the Act, it is not necessary to also prove that the food item had become unfit for human consumption or injurious to health.
In cases of food coming under the Act, it is not required to prove that article of food was injurious to health.
In this case, the only question to be determined is whether the article complies with the standards laid down or not?
If it fails to comply with the standards then it will have to be treated as an adulterated article even if it is not rendered injurious to health.

Even marginal deviation from the prescribed standard cannot be ignored."
10.
The bare perusal of the above judgments make it clear that the provisions of FSS Act needs strict interpretation.

The appellants have not disputed that the INS number was not mentioned on the Shri Rajmal Thakur S/O Late Shri Het Ram vs Food Safety Officer on 19 August, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/45818632/

sentences.text:
The complaint was filed against the appellants for the violation of Section 23(1), 26(1),
26(2)(ii), 27(1) and 27(2)(c) of FSS Act. Section 23(1) FSS Act

makes it mandatory that no person shall manufacture, distribute, sell or expose for sale or despatch or deliver to any agent or broker for the purpose of sale, any packaged food products which are not marked and labelled in the manner as may be specified by regulations.
Such regulation has been provided in Regulation 2.2.2.5(i) of FSS(P&L) Regulations.
Similarly, Section 26(1) FSS Act provides responsibilities of the food business operator.

It also cast a duty on the FBO to ensure that the articles of food satisfy the requirements of this Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder at all stages of production,
processing, import, distribution and sale within the businesses under his control.

Section 26 (2)(ii)
FSS Act also mandates that no food business operator shall himself or by any person on his behalf manufacture, store, sell or distribute any article of food which is misbranded or substandard or contains extraneous matter.

Section 27(1) FSS Act also provides liability of manufacturers, packers,
wholesalers, distributors and sellers.

It provides that the manufacturer or packer of an article of food shall be liable for such article of food if it does not meet the requirements of this Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder.

Section 27(2)
(c) FSS Act also provides that the wholesaler or distributor shall be liable under this Act for any article of food which is unsafe or misbranded.
11. In the present case, admittedly the INS number as required under regulation was not mentioned.

It does not lie in the mouth of appellants now to say that since there was no class II preservative,
therefore, nonmentioning of INS number has no significance.

Ld. ADM has passed a detailed,
reasoned order and has taken into account the judgments cited by the appellants and the submissions made by them.
Thus, it is quite apparent that there is a violation on the part of the appellants of Regulation No. 2.2.2.5(i) FSS (P&L) Regulations.
Therefore, the defence of due diligence also cannot be afforded to the appellants in view of specific provisions as provided under Section 26 & 27 FSS Act.
The provisions in Section 26 & 27 FSS Act are strict in nature and cast a duty on the FBO in no uncertain terms.
The judgments cited by the Ld. Counsel for the appellants are distinguishable in the facts and circumstances of the present case.
I consider that the same has rightly been distinguished by the Ld.ADM.
In view of the above facts and circumstances, I do not find any illegality in the impugned order dated 28.10.2019 passed by the Ld.ADM.
Hence, the appeal is dismissed.
12. Appeal file be consigned to Record Room.
